title: Authentication decorator fails open when authentication fails
description: require_auth catches Exception around both token parsing and abort(401), clears g.user, and then calls the protected view anyway. As a result, routes whose view does not dereference g.user can be accessed without authentication, and other protected routes may fail with an internal error rather than returning 401.
evidence: Code path: require_auth at shopapi/auth.py:48-59 catches abort(401) and returns f(*args, **kwargs). Requesting GET /orders/1 with an invalid Bearer token returned HTTP 200 and order 1's full details, even though show_order calls get_order() rather than checking ownership. This also defeats the intended authentication boundary for any similarly implemented route.

title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
description: show_order uses get_order rather than own_order. Any authenticated customer can retrieve another customer's order, including item quantities, payment totals, delivery date, and refunds; combined with the fail-open decorator, the tested endpoint also disclosed this data without valid authentication.
evidence: GET /orders/3 with a token for customer id 1 returned HTTP 200 and the order belonging to customer id 2. GET /orders/1 with Authorization: Bearer invalid also returned HTTP 200. The ownership check exists in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used by show_order.

title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False and only checks that the resulting subject maps to a user. An attacker can construct an unsigned token containing any known user id, including a staff user id, and receive a newly signed token for that account.
evidence: auth.py:101-107 uses jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) and then make_token(user). A request with an unsigned token containing sub=3 returned HTTP 200 and a signed token for the staff account id 3. That token can then authorize /admin routes.

title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
description: The basket cookie is entirely attacker-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads after base64 decoding. Python pickle deserialization can execute attacker-supplied __reduce__ payloads in the application process. This is reachable without authentication through GET /basket and the basket item endpoints.
evidence: basket.py:15-23 reads request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)); with_basket at lines 26-29 writes an unsigned, unencrypted pickle back to the client. No MAC/signature or safe serialization format is used.

title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL statement. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and potentially use SQLite-specific injection to disclose or manipulate data depending on the statement context.
evidence: products.py:40-42 builds SQL with "... LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." instead of parameters. GET /products/search?q=%25%27%20OR%201%3D1-- (q = %' OR 1=1--) returned all six products, whereas a normal search such as q=mug returns only MUG-SPECK.

title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML, enabling stored XSS
description: Review body input is stored without sanitization and is rendered with the Jinja safe filter. A customer can persist script or event-handler markup which executes whenever another user views the product page, including staff moderators.
evidence: products.py:82-91 stores the submitted body directly; templates/product.html:13 renders r.body|safe. There is no sanitizer for review bodies (description_html's bleach processing applies only to product descriptions).

title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment explicitly sets status='paid' and proceeds as though the provider confirmed payment. A customer can exploit provider/network availability or repeated timeout conditions to obtain an order marked processing without a successful payment.
evidence: payments.py:37-43 catches requests.Timeout and assigns status = "paid"; lines 43-46 then set the order to processing and paid_pence=total_pence. The comment says reconciliation happens later, but fulfillment is enabled immediately.

title: Payment webhook trusts an unauthenticated amount value
description: The webhook signature covers only order_id, not status or amount_pence. Anyone who obtains or can replay a valid order-id signature can submit a paid event with an arbitrary amount, and the handler records that amount as paid without comparing it with the order total or provider data.
evidence: webhook_signature at payments.py:53-55 signs only str(order_id). payment_webhook at lines 69-71 accepts int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) and writes it directly to paid_pence. There is no check that the amount equals total_pence, is positive, or is authenticated by the signature.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest, which is unsuitable for password storage. A database compromise permits efficient offline guessing and causes identical passwords to have identical hashes. Password reset and seeded accounts use the same weak scheme.
evidence: hash_password at auth.py:15-16 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), with no salt or work factor. The users schema stores only this value, and scripts/seed.py:32-33 creates demo accounts using it.

title: JWT signing secret is hardcoded in source
description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed literal in the repository. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployment artifact can forge HS256 authentication tokens, including staff tokens, and impersonate any user. The application also has a predictable default webhook secret.
evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" and config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to "whsec-local". JWTs are signed and verified with SECRET_KEY in auth.py:27 and auth.py:42.

title: Application is launched with Flask debug mode enabled
description: The normal run.py entry point calls app.run(debug=True). If this entry point is used in a reachable environment, Flask's debugger can expose detailed tracebacks and potentially its interactive debugger, which enables code execution when the debugger PIN is compromised or disabled/misconfigured.
evidence: run.py:5-6 invokes app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=True). This is the documented startup path in README.md:12.

title: Request logging records credentials and sensitive request bodies
description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is logged, truncated only at 2,000 characters. This includes login passwords, password-reset codes and new passwords, bearer-like values supplied in JSON, payment data, and other personal information. Anyone with log access can recover credentials or reset codes.
evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:29-31 logs request.get_data(as_text=True) for all state-changing requests without redaction. The login endpoint accepts passwords in POST JSON (auth.py:84-93), and reset confirmation accepts reset codes and new passwords (auth.py:143-159).
